body:
This seems to be working as intended to me. Freeing an object will cancel its suspended functions. `await some_func()` will only resume the function when `some_func` finishes. In this case `some_func` is canceled so the other coroutine does not get resumed.

It is not possible to resume the coroutine because code after the await might rely on results of the suspended function:

```gdscript
var a = await obj_will_get_freed.get_name()
print(a)
```

Freeing an object, canceling its coroutines is an understandable behavior. But if cancellation of coroutine can indefinitely suspend a call site, that makes debugging much harder than necessary without any good error/warning to go along with it. Some functions may need to do some necessary cleanup or run other critical code for the game after the await.

There are ways to circumvent this, like manually emitting a signal and awaiting the signal instead, but if the signal gets emitted on the same frame as the await then the await can still hang indefinitely. Also for Node objects, you can await tree exited signal, and race between the coroutine and the signal to continue to execution, but that's not ideal, since its specific to Node only, and godot doesn't provide methods to await the deletion of objects. Further more, racing coroutines isn't natively supported by gdscript, and the implementation isn't trivial.

Ideally, there'd be mechanism to detect and react to the cancellation of coroutines. But if that is not feasable, a warning or error if a canceled coroutine keeps a caller suspended indefinitely, would make debugging much easier.

Otherwise there could be an annotation to regress certain methods back to older behaviour where the coroutine will continue even after the owning object is freed.

Racing is just a concept from other programming languages with asynchronous programming support. Basically, you run multiple coroutine/async calls at the same time and return when atleast one is completed. An example being `Promise.race` from javascript.

From the solution that you provided, I can see that it is possible to react to the deletion of an object, so this is a very good solution to the problem. Though, again the solution isn't trivial.

I still do think a warning is warranted, for new people learning the language.
Those warning would be pretty annoying, because this is something that's wanted in most cases.

The warning would only happen if the coroutine is awaited and a the caller is suspended indeffinitely because of the owning object getting freed, not anytime an object is freed while a coroutine is taking place.

A potential unexpected deadlock feels like a significant error to me, coming from a web dev background. Of course game dev semantics can be different from that of web dev.

If such a warning would be undesirable and there isn't much more discussion to have here, this issue can be closed I think.
